utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, ma'am. All the accused are present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey alone. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic and the Beara team. So I take it there are no preliminaries? So Mr. Haynes, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Haynes [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, we left off yesterday afternoon on the 23rd of July when you heard -- had a meeting with Dragan Obrenovic following a briefing of the commanders at the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade. I just want to finish the events of the 23rd of July before retracing our steps to deal with an issue we were talking about just prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So if we can start, please, by having a look at the regular combat report for the 23rd of July, which is P341.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can see that under paragraph 1 is the usual description of the combat situation which reads: "At 2100 hours last night the Turks launched and infantry attack against the defence of the 3rd Battalion." And at 0045: "The enemy launched a strong infantry attack from behind the 2nd Infantry Company of the 4th Battalion." Using that as an aid-memoire, what was the general combat situation on the 23rd of July in the zone of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this report demonstrates the situation quite clearly. The first item talks about enemy activity, and that they were pronounced. The second item talks about the activities of the Zvornik Brigade in response to enemy activity. There were captured, also casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've drawn me on to the next point which is if we look at paragraph 3 of the report and in particular the last sentence we see it says: "20 enemy soldiers were killed today, and seven captured." Were you still, as it were, spending your days at the command in the barracks on the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the day there was a briefing and I spent most of the day at the command. First I just want to say that the information about the number of enemy soldiers who were killed might be exaggerated because we couldn't have known the exact number, but usually these were round numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in relation to those that were captured, is a regular combat report the only document in which the capture of enemy soldiers was recorded by the brigade, or was it recorded somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the information was noted in the duty operations log-book of the barracks, and that the duty officers also mentioned the information in his log-book. Possibly something was also written down in the operations diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come on to that in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page of this document, there's just one more aspect of it I'd like your comments on, which is paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It reads: "Requests: As requested by command organs. Requests relating to fuel and ammunition of all calibres should be considered particularly seriously. The MUP should be urgently requested for a unit to use in our brigade's area of responsibility by tomorrow, the 24th of July at 0600 hours at the latest." Why was it necessary to address that request to corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in the course of the 18th the MUP units, which were under my command, were leaving the Baljkovica area, and then the units of the public security centre in Zvornik were engaged under Vasic's command to carry out certain tasks of searching the terrain. This request probably refer to a coordination of the activities so that we would know who was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to conclude that day by looking at the duty officers' notebook, P377. If Ms. Stewart would be good enough to provide you again with the hard copy, you can look at pages 795 and 796. Those of us looking at e-court need to look at page 177 to start off with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a fairly straightforward point, if we look at the bottom of that page, General Pandurevic, we can see the familiar telephone number, 589-991 just before an entry at 2025. Does that help to refresh your memory as to what time on the 23rd of July you left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my habit that when I was in the brigade, any time I was outside of the brigade somewhere in Zvornik, I would leave the number where I would be, where I could be found. This is the number in Celopek where I spent my free time. And if this duty officer wrote down this in the proper sequence of events, then this would be the time of around 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that be the time about which you left on that evening?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just go over the page, please. Your 796, our 178.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's the entry just under the underlined portion about "Strbac, wake up at 0430," which says "chief's driver Vule at 0430 hours." Who was Vule, and to what does this appear to relate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can this is the driver of the Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic. I don't know his last name, this Vule, but what's written down here is that the operations officer was waking him up at 0430 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection now of whether Obrenovic remained at the barracks after you left on the 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I issued an assignment to Obrenovic to be in connection with the corps command and that pursuant to our request to begin resolving the question of the prisoners and their transport to Batkovic as soon as possible, to be in communication with Colonel Cerovic and as soon as he received instructions from him he was to start organising the transport of the prisoners of war to Batkovic. As I was leaving the barracks -- I mean, I left the barracks and from what I recall he stayed at the command, which doesn't mean that occasionally he could have been at some other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But prior to your departure on the 23rd of July, were you aware of any prisoners being transported away from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the day, but in the morning, at the morning briefing I found out that the first group of prisoners had gone to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's just, as it were, retrace our steps and deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I just wonder whether the witness has any comment on the entry which appears just before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Who was that "I."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the duty officer on the evening of the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that Ljubo Bojanovic was the duty officer and this entry that His Honour is speaking about is written with a different handwriting, so it could have been that it was the assistant duty operations officer of Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps most importantly, is it your comment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give any specific comment on this. I just listened to the testimony of Ljubo Bojanovic, and in the Jokic and Blagojevic case he said -- or he gave his comments on this entry. I could repeat it but this is not my direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you were to be reported by the duty operations officer later on, or you read these entries later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've never had this notebook in my hands before. I've never read it. The duty operations officer would report to me the most important details in view of this note that has to do with Skelani, and something that is quite outside of the scope and responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. I didn't know about this entry before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when this entry was written, and this call was taken?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entry could have been made during the night sometime or later, perhaps early in the morning, if you follow the sequence of entries and the times that they were made. At the time I was away, I was in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we were discussing -- we were going back to discuss the question of prisoners, and what happened to them at the Zvornik Brigade, and so on and so forth. We'll recall yesterday that you told us about the requests you made for arrangements to be made for the prisoner that is you were taking that began on the 20th of July, and proceeded through to the 23rd of July. Were you taking prisoners every day throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were prisoners. I'm not sure if this happened every day, but you can see that from the records and regular reports. From what I can remember, I think that on the 21st of July, there were no prisoners because fighting was going on at that time with the 2nd Corps forces who were attacking from the front, so there was no sweeping of the terrain. I think that there were prisoners captured in the other days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did prisoners begin to be transported out of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were they taken to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, within the brigade, what records were kept of the presence of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have the numbers here, the number of prisoners captured every day, but during the transport and their handover to the Batkovic collection centre, this had to be done according to a list, and I don't know where these lists are anymore because each prisoner who was transferred to Batkovic is recorded as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Probably my fault, General Pandurevic; probably not a very good question. But when prisoners arrived at the brigade, in what document was the number of prisoners noted?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the barracks duty operations officer was at the very entrance to the barracks, he would be the one to record the presence, the entry, the exit of all the persons, especially persons who did not belong to the brigade. So he would record the number of prisoners of war who would be brought to the barracks in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And let's just have a look at some examples of that. Can we have a look at P383, please. This document is not translated, so we are going have to look at page 16 firstly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we are going to need your help, General Pandurevic. And I wonder if you could -- I don't think we have the -- yes. I wonder if you could start reading the sentence which appears at the fifth bullet point on that page and read it sufficiently slowly and clearly for the interpreters to follow, would you, General Pandurevic, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all I would like to say that this is an entry of the barracks duty officer for the 22nd -- 23rd July of 1995. And it contains the usual information, and the sentence on which you insist states: "During the afternoon and the night, about 30 enemy soldiers were brought to the barracks." The duty officer was Zoran Begovic, he was a doctor head of the medical section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we now go to page 18 in the same document, the barracks duty officers' log-book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the entry for the 24th and the 25th of July, I think we can all see that from the top. And I'd like you to read the sentences beginning five lines from the bottom, and if you could again identify who the barracks duty officer was who made the entry?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Bogdanovic was the duty officer, and it says: "During the shift, 29 Muslim soldiers were captured and brought to the barracks by the military police of the eastern corps. 20 Muslim soldiers were brought in."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that of course is an internal record. We've already seen several daily combat reports, but was it the practice of the brigade to report to corps command the existence of the number of prisoners on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would be contained in the regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's complete the picture there then, please. Can we have a look at P342.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the regular combat report for the 24th of July, and for present purposes I'm only interested in the last sentence of paragraph 3 which reads: "Fourteen enemy soldiers have been captured today." Was that, as it were, standard practice to include that information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the number was entered that the operations officer knew of by the time he sent the report. Sometimes after the report was sent some more were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any reason in July of 1995 in particular after the 16th of July of 1995 that you thought you shouldn't be reporting that to corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for that. My position was that every soldier who surrendered had to be sent to the prisoner of war collection centre and the corps command should be made aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This might seem an obvious question given your answer to the last one, but did you see any reason why you shouldn't be taking prisoners of war during this period?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to search the ground and everybody who was captured during the search was brought to the barracks. There was no reason to treat soldiers contrary to the Geneva Conventions and regulations on the application of the Laws of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to P344, the daily combat report for the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, it's the last sentence of paragraph 3 of that report: "Twenty-five enemy soldiers were captured. All were duty transferred to the Batkovici-Bijeljina collection centre." Can you help us just by glancing at the second page of that report as to which duty officer wrote that report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could this be scrolled down just a little, I need to inspect the initials on this page. I believe that the initials that I see here are MG, standing for Mihajlo Galic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly, P346, the daily combat report for the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to confound us, the information about prisoners is not in paragraph 3 of this report, but paragraph 2, it's the fourth bullet point: "The reconnaissance group of the 1st Birac Brigade combed the terrain in the area of Kozluk; 34 members of the BH Army were captured and sent to the prison in Batkovici." Again, if you can help us please by going to page 2 of this report and giving us the name, if you can, of the duty officer who wrote that report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials are JP. You would have to give me a minute to think who that might be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's probably not that important, Mr. Pandurevic, but certainly --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to look at the list of the brigade command, that would jog my memory. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So the position throughout this period was the arrival of prisoners was recorded in the barracks duty officers' notebook. The figures in the regular combat report seem to be rather more accurate, does the duty officer then go and count them before he writes his report to corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the duty officer went to count head. He probably obtained information from the barracks duty officer or from the individuals who had brought the prisoners in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- but in any event a record is made in a daily combat report and is sent to corps command on a daily basis of the number of prisoners taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from about the 20th of July, you began beseeching corps command to make arrangements for you to exchange all these prisoners you were taking; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you've already hinted at, their reception at the collection centre at Batkovici is also recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we are going to have a look now to a document that is not a Zvornik Brigade document. It's 7D712, and I think this document better not be broadcast because it contains names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. If there is any objection to the blocking of the broadcast, please speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document with a number of pages and flicking through it on e-court will be time consuming, so I'm going to hand you a hard copy with the assistance of Eva. Thank you very much. Now, you've told us that prisoners began to leave the Zvornik Brigade on the 23rd of July. I know you've been through this document. How many prisoners were transferred from the Zvornik Brigade to Batkovici between the 23rd and the 26th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several columns here in the list in addition to the name, the family name, and the particulars of every individual. There's also the date of their arrival in Batkovic collection centre, and as far as I can remember between 23rd and 26th of July, between 140 and 150 prisoners of war were transferred there after having been captured by the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am just being informed, Mr. Haynes, and Mr. McCloskey and the rest, that this document actually was tendered by the Prosecution, and it is not confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then, in that case it can be broadcast. And for those who want to see it, it might be better that they have a look at page 2 so they can see what General Pandurevic is referring to. I had it in my mind, I didn't check that there were some names on this that caused it to be used under seal, but if I'm wrong, I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Thayer used it with Novica Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- just to recall everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can proceed then, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as you are aware those 140 or 150 prisoners, how were they treated when they were at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My order was to treat them correctly, fairly. We have been faced with different statements here. Some said that they were treated fairly, the others said that the treatment was not fair. I don't have a clear insight. I don't have a precise information as to how each of the soldiers treated them in the woods when capturing them. However, when they arrived in the barracks, they received fair treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on average how long would a prisoner have remained at the Zvornik Brigade before being transferred to the collection centre at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the -- those who came first stayed the longest until the moment the operation to transfer them to Batkovici was launched, and then those who were captured during the day, as soon as there was a truck-load, they would be transported to Batkovic on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, against that background, I think I just ought to put to you a couple of paragraphs of the indictment. There were apparently 11 wounded prisoner who came from a hospital in Milici at the command of the Zvornik Brigade at some stage. What did you know about the existence of those persons?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about their existence when I returned from the IKM. I can't tell you exactly when that was, whether that was on the 18th or the 19th, because I don't remember. However, as soon as I received the information, as soon as I learned that there were such people there, I was not really clear why the wounded had to be accommodated in the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade together with the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade who had been wounded, and I personally ordered Dragan Obrenovic to inspect them and to look after their safety and that that order should be conveyed to the medical personnel. My order was to treat the enemy wounded as any other wounded person would be treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as you're aware, on what date did they leave the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted with Colonel Cerovic that the wounded should also be transferred from the Zvornik Brigade. At the morning briefing on the 24th, Dragan Obrenovic reported that together with the other prisoners they were also transported to the Batkovic collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you were talking to Mr. Cerovic about in the intercepted communication we looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, did you order or authorise the execution of those wounded prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade infirmary?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order or authorise the execution of any prisoners who were held in the barracks at the Zvornik Brigade during the latter part of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been crazy on my part. It would have been crazy to capture somebody, to bring him to the barracks, and then execute him. I never issued an order to that effect. And as far as I know, nobody was allowed or permitted to execute a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the 15th of July, did you ever participate in further combat operations towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in any operations. However, I did spend sometime in the Zepa area after the 15th. That happened on two occasions, if I remember it correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's take them one by one. After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, since you are moving away from the topic, if I can raise the -- raise a point that I wanted to yesterday but I couldn't due to the time constraint. Can I draw your attention to yesterday's page 31154. You put the witness the question: "What sort of mood were you in when you had this discussion with Obrenovic?" And in the course of answering this question, Mr. Pandurevic said, I quote: "It was our conclusion to the effect that where is this leading us, what sort of a brain could have decided something like that." And then he said: "But according to the information that we had, we knew that the order had come from General Mladic." I'm interested to know what kind of information he had and how he came to the conclusion that it had come from General Mladic. I would like the witness to expand on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to interfere in that question. He can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Pandurevic can answer the question directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received initial information from Dragan Obrenovic and he had received that information on the 14th in the evening when he was at the command of the Zvornik Brigade and when he was sending that interim combat report. And even earlier than that, Nikolic had told him in a conversation that those prisoners were being brought in pursuant to an order of the commander of the Main Staff. I did not have any direct information. The commander of the Main Staff never issued such an order to me. However, I assumed that no such thing could have been done or the transport of prisoners carried out from one territory to another territory with the engagement of the security organs and the security escorts without that. I can have my doubts about the information that the order came from Mladic or not. However, in light of the subsequent events and the fact that no measures were taken, I'm still convinced that the order did indeed come from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the 15th of July, when was the first time that you went back to the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I returned around the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can use something to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at 7D91.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a form of document with which we are all very familiar now. This is a vehicle work log and it relates to a vehicle we are pretty familiar with, the Nissan T-2175, the car in which you were driven around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the fourth page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see there on the 27th of July that the car is recorded as going from Zvornik to Vlasenica. Is that where its journey ended on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm told that the page in B/C/S is page 3, not page 4 as it is in the English. Apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was not the final destination on that day. I proceeded to IKM Godjenje from Vlasenica, and there I met with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you had for some time wanted to speak to him face to face. Why did you not go before the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 23rd, it was certain that some elements of the Zvornik Brigade that had previously been engaged in Zepa area would be sent back, and that's why you see the note here for the 23rd of July, Zvornik-Han Pijesak-Zepa. This was noted by the driver because I thought that I would indeed be going to Zepa on that. However, everything was put on hold. We were informed to stand by and not to move, so we remained on standby for several days. I had several conversations with Cerovic, Jevdjevic, and Krstic, I believe. And finally I left without any units on my own on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll just, as it were, have a look at a few extraneous documents to illustrate what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D602, please. A in the English, B in B/C/S. Thank you. Yes, it's been pointed out to me that this in fact is an exhibit under a different number. It's P1194.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is an intercept from the 23rd of July between Zlatar corps command and Palma and Zvornik Brigade. "Give me Palma." "Sorry?" "Palma." "Just a moment." "Is that Palma?" "Give me 01." Who would 01 at Palma be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are looking at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We need A and B. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The numeral 01, who would that refer to at Zlatar and who would that refer to at Palma?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatar 1 was General Krstic, and Palma 1 would be me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes, did you say that the date of this intercept is 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can we deduce is going on from this intercepted communication, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Our records indicate this intercept is the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, will you verify that, please, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's tied up to a previous question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which specifically referred to the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, we'll move on. We'll go to 7D604 which is probably a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this intercept is, I believe, the 25th of July, and it's between Cerovic, about whom we've heard a good deal in the last few days, and a general. You were in contact with Cerovic during this period, did you receive any information or instruction from him as to what state of readiness you should be in in relation to any particular operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in contact with Cerovic, and it had to do with my return to the Zepa area. And then from the 23rd on he was telling me every day to be ready, to wait for the order that Krstic was supposed today issue, and this is also what this conversation is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to P1353. A in the English, and B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to hand you a hard copy, General Pandurevic, because in the B/C/S it starts at the bottom of the first page and goes over two more pages, so it will be easier for you to leaf through a hard copy. This is an intercept from 8.00 in the morning of the 26th of July. It's a fairly long intercept. Once you've got the text of it perhaps you can tell us whether you recall speaking to Major Jevdevic on the morning of the 26th of July and what you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this conversation. I was asking about whether I would be requested to return to Zepa. I asked Jevdevic what the situation was, and he told me that probably they were not going to ask me to go back because he said the guns have been silent for the second day now, meaning that the fighting had stopped and that preparations were underway, or already the evacuation was underway in Zepa. And he said that I was requested only where the guns were active, meaning only where there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to complete that particular picture, can we see 7D609, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again an intercept from the 26th of July at 2320 in the evening. A conversation apparently between the duty operations officer at Palma and Zlatar, and you, but it begins curiously by: "Vinko is not in at the moment. Who wants to talk to him? "Zlatar. "Hello. Just a moment, just a moment. "Yes. "Chief, how are you? "Well, not bad. I feel relieved just talking to you. Listen. "Yes, I'm listening. "Uran 01 told me that you should be here, in, at this where we were located previously. "Please repeat. "At 0800 in the morning." Do you recall having a conversation in the late evening of the 26th of July with somebody from the corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is another part of this conversation. If I can look at it, please, so that I could have a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this conversation, and it demonstrates that I was supposed to report to the IKM where Krstic was the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the principal purpose of your visit to General Krstic on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason was to talk to him about my interim combat reports of the 15th, 16th, and the 18th. And the second reason was that I think that by that time already an order had arrived to send a unit from the Drina Corps to the 2nd Krajina Corps and that the Zvornik Brigade was obliged to allocate forces for that purpose, the equivalent of a battalion, so this was another thing that I wanted to speak to him about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there alone?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went with a driver. Probably somebody was also escorting me and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where precisely did you go to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I met Krstic at the forward command post in the village of Godjenje, and that in the course of the day I stopped off in Vlasenica to see Zvonko Bajagic [Realtime transcript read in error "Blagojevic"]. I don't know whether this was before I saw Krstic or afterwards. I'm not sure about that. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we can have a look at the another document. You've got the duty officers' notebook, if you go to page 885 where you are, and we look at page 187 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to clear up, he went to see a person named Bajagic not Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the first page of the duty operations officers' notebook for the 27th of July, and we see three lines up from the bottom "Commander Bajagic in Vlasenica," is that the name as it should be recorded in the transcript, B-a-j-a-g-i-c?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what time you got to Godjenje?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was early in the morning that I left the command. How early, I'm not sure. But by noon I had probably finished my conversation with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody else at the forward command post on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was a tent there. The commander of the headquarters administration of the Drina Corps, I think his name was Amovic was there. And then Jevdjevic who was chief of the communications, some communications operators, maybe messengers, General Krstic's driver. I don't know any of their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and Krstic talk alone?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that within the tent or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a nice day from what I can remember. There was some sort of fence in front of the tent, perhaps we were standing next to that fence and we were talking. I think that's where it was. First, General Krstic asked me about the situation in the Zvornik Brigade, about the situation in the area of defence, and then I addressed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, Probably you received my interim combat reports, which I sent you, and in which I mentioned what I mention in them. And I asked him if he had any more specific and broader information than the one I stated in the combat reports relating to the prisoners of war who were executed in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said something to the effect that, Hey Vinko, I know something that shouldn't have happened happened. I don't even know myself how it all started but I do know what happened, and I know who was included in that and who did that, but this is something that should not be your concern. I am going to deal with this problem in the appropriate way. I para-phrased what he told me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you talk about this for?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a long conversation. Maybe we talked for ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss your orders in relation to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the situation was critical in the western part of Republika Srpska in the 2nd Krajina Corps section, he said that he knew what the situation was in the Zvornik Brigade in terms of its effort and the stretching of the men in the fighting, but that I had to find a solution and allocate the forces that were being requested of me and send them to the sector of the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that part of the conversation by the fence, or did that discussion take part somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the conversations took place at the same location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you help us now as to which came first. Did you start talking about your interim combat reports, or did you start talking about your orders to go to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since General Krstic first asked me about the situation in the area of the brigade and the situation in the brigade, I then touched upon my interim combat reports and then this Krajina topic was the last one in the sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was going on in the Zepa area on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were no combat actions. I think that the evacuation of the civilian population was underway, but I didn't have specific information about the manner in which this was being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any unit of the Zvornik Brigade return to Zepa after the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of July after my conversation with General Krstic, it seemed as if no units would be required to go from the Zvornik Brigade, but as far as I can remember later a number of the Podrinje Detachment of the special forces left to the Zepa broader sector. I think this was on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how long they stayed there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a number of them returned the following day, that a number stayed for another two days because then on the 3rd of August the order was received to form another Drina Brigade that would be sent to the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps so that the engagement of those forces of the Podrinje Detachment in the Zepa area was not required. They went, just stayed there for a short period of time, and then returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. Well, I just want to sweep up a couple of documents before the break. Can we have a look at P379. This is the later duty operations officers' log-book. It's an entry for the 2nd of August. And for present purposes, we'll just look at it in e-court, General Pandurevic. That's page 19 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the 2nd of August, and I'm interested in you helping us with what the entry at 2046 refers to.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legenda checked in after coming back from Zepa, and that one of his platoons remained up there. This means that the commander of the Podrinje Detachment, Milan Jolovic, came back from Zepa at this time and that he informed the duty officer that a platoon of his unit stayed in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did it stay after Legenda got back?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the platoon came back the following day because the entire Podrinje Detachment became part of the 2nd Drina Brigade headed by me, and we went to the area of the Krajina Corps. The order on its establishment was issued on the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to conclude this period, P349. Daily combat report for the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's the third bullet point under paragraph 2 I'm interested in where it says: "A unit is being prepared, as ordered by the KDK Drina Corps command. Order strictly confidential number 33/95 dated the 26th of July, 1995. "In order for it to be able to set out on its assignment, the unit needs to be supplied with:" And fuel and ammunition is thereafter listed. What order does that refer to and what unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the Drina Corps command to send a brigade to the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps. The Zvornik Brigade was supposed to provide one battalion, and I actually discussed this with General Krstic when we met on the 27th. As far as I can remember, the commander of that battalion was Ljubo Bojanovic, because I also met them later at one time in the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And if that's convenient, we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now of 25 minutes duration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, forgive me, we are going to retrace our steps a little bit. Not because it helps the narrative, but really just because I don't like people to think I've made a mistake. I did mean to call into e-court 7D602, and it does have a P number. It was the P number I was erroneously informed of. The P number is the P1314 A in the English and B in the B/C/S. So if we could have that put into e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this now is an intercept of the 23rd of July timed at about 1132 in the morning. Apparently between General Krstic and Colonel Cerovic, and really it's the bottom portion of it that we are concerned with where General Krstic apparently says to Cerovic: "Go on, call Vinko. "Yes. "And if it's possible, he should personally come here to see me. "Yes, sir. "If it's possible, if the situation permits. "Okay. "Not tomorrow, but today. "Okay. "Good-bye." Did you receive a message on the 23rd of July that General Krstic wanted to see you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most probably did and here he kind of made it conditional if possible that I should go and see him on that day. I didn't come across any conversation with me discussing this topic with Cerovic, but probably there was a conversation between Cerovic and myself, and that that day I didn't go. The briefing was held at the brigade command that day, and that day was the day that I signed the regular combat report, meaning that I was there that whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's just have a look at P341 again, please. And we need to look at the bottom of the document in Serbian. The next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that's not actually type signed, it's got a signature on it. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. My initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to complete the history, can we have a look, please, at 7D607.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Colonel Cerovic and General Krstic at 25 past 5.00 in the afternoon of the 26th of July: "Did you call Vinko?" "Excuse me?" "Did you call ... ?" "Yes." "You did." "Milenko says he will be up there at 0800 in the morning." This appears to follow on from the other intercept -- intercept we've looked at between you and Jevdjevic. Did you tell Jevdjevic that you would attend General Krstic at 8.00 on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll leave that behind us now finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now have in e-court, please, 7D729.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another marching order, and you've explained to us what the effect of such a document is. What unit did you give a marching order to on the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the document, pursuant to an order of the Drina Corps of the 26th of July, the Zvornik Brigade formed from among its ranks one light infantry battalion which became part of the Drina Brigade force, and this is an order for the battalion to march. The battalion that was going to become a part of the Drina Brigade of the Drina Corps. And it was written on the 26th of July, and it was being sent to the sector of operation of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the marching order that relates to the unit you told us about before the break commanded by Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see at the beginning that the commander of the first echelon was Captain Maric. As far as I can recall Ljubo Bojanovic was the commander of the battalion because I met him at a facility at Crni Vrh in the Glamoc sector. Perhaps his name is also mentioned here, but I don't see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll move on from that, please, to P351.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 28th of July, you felt the need to send an interim combat report. Why?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informing the corps command that we had acted pursuant to their order, that we had executed the order, and we cited the MTS and the number of people involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see that was 220. Is that the number of soldiers that you dispatched?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is says here. Probably that was the number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just one more piece in the jigsaw before we pull this all together. P124, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a Drina Corps order preparing units of the corps for full combat readiness, described as very urgent. What is this document about and what situation militarily does it reflect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here the commander of the Drina Corps issues an order based on the order of the Main Staff on raising the level of combat morale, or, as it says here, literally putting corps units into full combat readiness. Now, this full combat readiness implies the immediate readiness of the units for the combat operations. In the last paragraph this is corroborated by the fact that the president of the republic also proclaimed a state of war in Republika Srpska. That mere fact made the situation serious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was going on at this time that created such a serious situation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was critical in the western part of Republika Srpska at that moment. That situation had been caused by the attacks of the Croatian army against Republika Srpska Krajina during Operation Storm. Those attacks and the negative effects on the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina spilled over to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing from the 29th of July onwards?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acted in keeping with the order that we have on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did that mean you were engaged in day-to-day?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to tour the battalions and inspect them. I was supposed to issue very clear tasks to the battalion commanders. And this meant that new forces would be necessary from the Drina Corps to be dispatched into the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now go to 7D615, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order of the Drina Corps dated the 3rd of August pursuant to an order of the Main Staff forming a brigade of which you were the commander. When did you first learn that you were to be the commander of a brigade to go to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly whether the meeting took place on the 3rd of August at the corps command or maybe it was on the 2nd. In any case, it referred to the obligations of the brigades of the Drina Corps to allocate men and form the 2nd Drina Brigade to be sent into the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. But I remember that initially Lieutenant-Colonel Radomir Furtula was appointed as its commander, he had been commander of the 5th Podrinje Brigade. However, when I arrived as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, I got a telephone call from Krstic who told me that Furtula had become ill all of a sudden and that I would have to serve as the brigade commander. Obviously I accepted the order and that's why it says in this order that was to be appointed the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this order take effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took effect on the day when it was issued, and it implied launching all the activities with a view to establishing a brigade. As you can see, this brigade was formed from the elements of all the brigades of the Drina Corps and such units are most difficult for command because they are very different, men are of different providences, of different opinions and views, with different equipment and armament. Such units are very difficult to use in combat and very difficult to control and command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to direct your attention to a couple of paragraphs of this order. Can you have a look, please, at paragraph 1 sub-paragraph (b). What does it mean "headquarters administration staff to be provided by the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every brigade has headquarters administration. This is a small unit that serves the command, and the command of the Zvornik Brigade, i.e., the Zvornik Brigade was supposed to establish the headquarters administration for the new brigade and was also supposed to establish a 250-men strong battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do between the 3rd and 7th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after having received this order, I was duty-bound to proceed accordingly. I was in constant communication with all the other brigade commanders from the Drina Corps with a view to efficiently gather all the men, materiel, technical equipment, and to establish first the command and finally the entire brigade. In that sense, I started issuing my first orders to that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my office from which I had commanded the Zvornik Brigade previously which means that I didn't move. My office did not move. I assumed my new duty, but I retained the same office and Dragan Obrenovic took over from me, and he was in command of the Zvornik Brigade. He performed his duties from his own office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the moment of this order, what function did you have within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was no longer the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. It was never officially confirmed. I did not receive any orders to that effect in writing, but the fact I was no longer the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just before we pass from this document, can we have a look at the last paragraph of it, which is page 2 I think in both documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in paragraph 10: "All other matters which are not regulated by this order, shall be regulated by the commander of the newly-formed brigade." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that I have to make sure that all the other issues that regard the establishment of the brigade and its preparation for use are to be regulated by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to 7D611, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order of yours dated the 3rd of August. Can you tell us what effect this order had or what its purpose was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued this order pursuant to the last paragraph of the previous order of the corps commander, and I sent it to the commands of all the corps brigades. It was not for me to order the commanders of the other brigades. I just insisted on the implementation of all the things that the corps commander wanted to do and institute all the other elements that would enable the brigade to carry out the tasks given to it by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see at the foot of the document, which might be quite difficult for you to read in the original, three time stamps: 1215, 1330, and 1750. Do you recall what time of day you issued this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp is not legible and it's very difficult for me to detect the initial time. But it is possible that it was 1750 when the document was drafted and sent for encryption. The next time is 1730, that's when it was processed by the encryptor, and last time, 1750, is the time when the document arrived at the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, at the time that you were ordered to command this brigade, was there any anticipated period that you would be in command of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became the commander of the brigade on the 3rd of August, 1995, as you can see in General Krstic's order. And on that same day, as you can see, I was in full command of that brigade which was still under establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how long did you think you would hold that position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on previous practice, one would expect not to stay in such a position long. Up to 15 days at the most. However, later on it turned out that the brigade had spent over a month in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we looked at various military documents at the beginning of your testimony, but if Dragan Obrenovic became acting commander of the brigade from the 3rd of August, was there any automatic ascension to the role of Chief of Staff from within the ranks of the other officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Could we first establish who, if anyone, became acting commander of the brigade before we ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we already have, haven't we? He has given volumes of evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. I think we can proceed. Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll phrase the question another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I think we can safely proceed in any case, but if you can phrase it in another way, maybe that's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the brigade formation provide for somebody automatically to become Chief of Staff if the Chief of Staff was no longer fulfilling that function?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll start with the principle of the singleness of command and unity of command. At the moment when I was appointed a commander of the 2nd Drina Brigade of the Drina Corps, somebody automatically had to take over the command of the Zvornik Brigade. By establishment and pursuant this had already been regulated. The Chief of Staff as the deputy commander was the one who would assume that position, and Obrenovic was that person. It was possible for appointing a new person that would be chair -- acting as Chief of Staff, but it was not mandatory. In this particular situation, as far as I can remember, and I'm sure that General Krstic had more information about the situation in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps and how long I would be required to stay there, and he decided to issue a new order after a few days. And by that new order, he appointed Dragan Obrenovic as the acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade. I believe that he also put in that order that Milos Maksimovic would be acting as the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade. This means that General Krstic at that time, unlike General Zivanovic, honoured the legal procedure, he complied with it and provided Obrenovic with all the necessary papers that would entitle him to all the benefits when he acted as commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, but I think we need to look with a little care at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so we'll put into e-court please 5D452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, this document is under seal I'm informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If it is, I'm very sorry for not spotting that. I can't imagine why it is, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't got a clue, but it is. Let's not broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, we have to be cautious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the order you're referring to. And firstly, can we note the date of it, it's the 8th of August, so five days after you became commander of the Drina Brigade. And it reads: "Order as acting for the war time establishment of Chief of Staff, at the same time deputy commander of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Milos Maksimovic, son of Cedo, artillery captain first class, born on the 17th of January 1963. Currently chief of artillery in the organ for the combat arms of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade of the Drina Corps. The duty pursuant to this order is to be taken over on the 8th August 1995 until the return on duty of the formation chief of brigade staff and will not be longer than six months. While acting as above, he will not carry out his formation duty and the brigade command will issue an order which will determine who will take on the duty of the above named." Then underneath it says: "Statement of reasons." What's the effect of this order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic issued this order pursuant to the Law on the Military. Dragan Obrenovic could not perform the duties of the Chief of Staff since he had been appointed as acting commander. That's why General Krstic decided to appoint Milos Maksimovic as acting Chief of Staff. Since we are talking about an establishment position that is usually taken by a lieutenant-colonel or colonel, Obrenovic cannot regulate who would assume the position of the Chief of Staff. It has to be the corps command to do that. The brigade commander either acting as or formerly the brigade commander can regulate by an order the appointment of officers to the positions occupied by majors or lieutenant-colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to another document now, please. 7D462.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have looked at this order together before, but just remind us what this is and what you say the effect of it is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, General Zivanovic corps commander is referring to paragraph 4(c) of the order issued by the minister of defence of Republika Srpska about the partisan authorities of officers. This order says the corps commander has the right and is authorised to appoint officers to establishment posts occupied by lieutenant-colonels or colonels, and here he appoints Dragan Obrenovic as Chief of Staff and at the same time deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I just want to look with you now at the situation between the 3rd and the 7th of August when, as you've told us, you were sitting in the office of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade commanding the Drina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we start, please, by looking at P360, the regular combat report for the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you might like just to read through the first page and then we'll go to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then with -- thank you. And just read those few lines. Whose signature is that on that document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in your office at the Zvornik Brigade at about 5.00 on the afternoon of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the time I was there as the commander of the 2nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any contribution to the writing of this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move on to P361, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the regular combat report of the following day, the 5th of August. Again, if you'd just care to read through the first page and let us know when you are done and we can move forward one page.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again we could probably see for ourselves whose signature it is, but do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there and available to sign this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was probably in my office or around minding my own business. If I was duty-bound to sign this, I would have, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We probably all noticed that in the previous document, P360, the little two letters "ZA," "za," had been put in front of the commander, meaning for the commander. On this document it's not been put in. Is there any significance in that one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's look at, please, P2839 [Realtime transcript read in error "P3829"]. And thankfully this is a one-page document so we can deal with it a bit quicker. I'm sorry, it's come up wrong in the transcript. 2839.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, just confirm to us that you can recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the very beginning I recognise Dragan Obrenovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing on the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was marching with my brigade from Zvornik to Bijeljina and onwards to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any significance in the fact we've got yet a third variation in the way that it's signed this time, standing in for the commander Major Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of responsibility and powers, no. In terms of status issues and the status of Dragan Obrenovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, if I could just interrupt you for a moment. I think on line 22, page 39 [sic]. That should be the 6th of August. It wouldn't make sense otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you leave to the Krajina with the Drinski Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I left on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your point of departure?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column was formed in Kozluk north of Zvornik some 12 to 15 kilometres away from Zvornik. That was our departure point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just interested because I think in answer to my question a little earlier about what you were doing on the 6th of August, you said you were marching. Where were you marching on the 6th of August, if indeed you were?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you asked me about the 8th of August and I was marching on that day, on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were you on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th I was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you experience on your march from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the hardest march any unit under my command ever took. On the one hand the column was very long and composed of various combat and non-combat vehicles in different sorts and states of repair, and the roads were overcrowded by a huge long column of refugees from the Republika Srpska Krajina. It's head in Bijeljina, that's where I first came across all these people, and they continued blocking our marching route throughout our march.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it took us the whole day on the 7th and then on the 8th, and on the 9th early in the morning, I arrived at the forward command post of the Main Staff and the 2nd Krajina Corps which was on Ostrezj pass midway between Petrovac and Drvar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what orders did you receive when you got there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Generals Mladic and Milovanovic there. I told them about the unit that I was leading and very soon thereafter I was issued a written order by General Milovanovic specifying certain axis of the use of the brigade from Drvar across Grahovo field and further on in the direction of Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you receive that task or those orders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was sometime in the morning at dawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you act upon those orders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back then and I was at the head of the column and I organised the subdivision of the combat disposition of the brigade and the launching of combat. We passed Drvar, we came to the edge of Grahovsko Polje and the same day we actually joined combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that combat last?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intense fighting lasted for two days and one night, and together with some other forces of the 2nd Krajina Corps we managed to stop the Croatian army from breaking through and to push them back to Grahovo. Later the front did not move more or less, the line of the front. And individual fighting was going on for the next 20 days or so, but sometime in late August, the fighting intensified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the state of the unit you commanded?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to evaluate the state of the unit because each battalion presented a separate problem. The unit of the Podrinje Detachment of the special forces was the most compact and parts of the units of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. The rest of the units were quite problematic, and an entire company from the Birac Brigade from Sekovici deserted after some ten days of combat and they returned to Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the calibre of the forces you were facing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were extremely strong forces of the guards brigade of the Croatian army supported by artillery and the air force. The artillery was active almost continuously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the end of August when combat intensified?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of August until mid-September, the gradual withdrawal of the forces of the 2nd Krajina Corps began, including the brigade that I commanded. And then later the withdrawal of the 2nd Krajina Corps took place all the way to the town of Kljuc, and this proceeded in a disorganised manner so that Petrovac was captured by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer losses in your unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were losses, and they were recorded separately for each battalion in view of the fact that the battalions were from different brigades. This was the stage of the war, or the year when it was decided to bring the war to an end, so all the warring parties were out to get the biggest possible piece of pie, or rather, to capture as much territory as they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to look briefly with you at two records of your period in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we look first, please, at 7D439.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, tell us what this document is, General Pandurevic, would you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that I drafted together with Mijo Dragutinovic who was an operations officer in this brigade. I think this is a document of some 15 to 16 pages where we presented the entire engagement of the 2nd Drina Brigade in detail and completely. We talked about the positive and the negative sides and experiences. We made certain proposals to overcome these problems, and the worst thing is that in 1995 we were faced with similar control and command problems as those in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's quite a chronological document. So I just want to pick through it quickly with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 8 in the English, which is page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here you're referring two-thirds of the way down the page in English, but in the top quarter of the page in B/C/S to a withdrawal from Grahovsko Polje on the 16th of August. What was the significance of that event?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an important event. There was an irregular and disorganised pullout of parts of the brigade, and at that point in time I happened to be at a very high mountain range over 1500 metres altitude with a battalion -- with one battalion, and to the left wing the attack by Croatian forces began and there was a disorganised withdrawal of one battalion so that we were practically cut off, and we managed to pull out at the last moment. But one company stayed behind in the enemy disposition and in the course of the night, they managed to withdraw without losses. Major Dragutinovic was with that company that was left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go over one page in the English, please, to page 9, but keep the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There you deal in the first large paragraph in the English page 9, but in the second half of the page in the B/C/S version with events between the 16th and 19th of August and going ton the 22nd of August. Again, briefly just explain to us how events developed during that period?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are events relating to the pullout of the brigade and its reaching new defence positions. We occupied quite strong facilities above the town of Drvar itself.
